tagline: From Kenai Lake to the road's end on Homer Spit.
intro: The Sterling leaves the Seward Highway at Tern Lake Junction and runs west beside the ice blue-green water of Kenai Lake to Cooper Landing, then plays tag with the Kenai River, a sportfishing water where the Russian River comes in. The byway is drawn here in two pieces, that north segment and a south segment that follows the Cook Inlet shore, with four volcanoes across the water, through Anchor Point to Homer and the tip of Homer Spit.
Work began in 1946. The highway opened in the winter of 1950, when the cold made it possible to drive the unfinished surface, and it needed grading and gravel before it was ready for summer traffic.

moments.title: Cooper Landing
moments.text: Named for Joseph Cooper, who found gold here in 1884, the settlement at the outlet of Kenai Lake counted 21 miners and one wife in the census of 1900.

moments.title: Anchor Point
moments.text: Named, the legend goes, for an anchor Captain Cook lost here, the town is the westernmost point on the North American highway system.

moments.title: Homer Spit
moments.text: The highway ends 4.5 miles out into Kachemak Bay, on a spit where an 1899 railroad hauling coal to the docks started the business that grew into Homer.
